If you use Google Chrome, take a few seconds today to check your settings and trigger an update. Google just rushed out an emergency fix for a critical sandbox escape vulnerability.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-134401, stems from improper input validation in the Chrome Variations component. A remote attacker could trick you into visiting a crafted webpage, bypass the browser sandbox completely, and run arbitrary code to grab your local files or sensitive data.

Google rolled out desktop versions 158.0.8127.88 and 89 across Windows, macOS, and Linux to seal the hole. Browsers usually wait for a full restart to apply patches, so it is genuinely worth bouncing the app manually before browsing anything suspicious.

Palo Alto Networks published advisory PAN-SA-2026-0015 on November 25 for Fragnesia, CVE-2026-46300 — a Linux kernel privilege-escalation flaw in the XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem, first disclosed in May 2026. On its own it needs a local foothold. The campaign chained it with PHP2Shell, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, PHP flaws that give remote code execution through the PAN-OS management web server — and then Fragnesia escalates that to root, all in a single HTTP request. Dream reported on October 26 that a Chinese-speaking, suspected China-nexus actor compromised 25 servers — 24 firewalls and one internal firewall management server — including two servers belonging to a U.S. government-affiliated organization, in an AI-assisted campaign on October 23–24. Palo Alto's Unit 42 verified the findings on October 29. The fix builds are out now, and Palo Alto says the only known PAN-OS route requires first exploiting PHP2Shell through an internet-exposed management interface — if you are running a fixed PAN-OS from the PHP2Shell advisory, you are protected.

I want to be precise about where the attribution comes from: the China link and the AI-assisted description are Dream's assessment, verified in scope by Palo Alto — Palo Alto's own advisory names no actor and does not mention AI. The number that should stay with you is the exposure figure Unit 42 gave: about 0.02 percent of customer devices worldwide had management interfaces exposed to the internet and were affected. Small in percentage, and every one of them was a firewall whose management plane was reachable from anywhere. The PHP2Shell patches were out by October 30; the Fragnesia fix lands today. If your management interface faces the internet, the patch is not the first thing to fix — the exposure is.

The management interface is the firewall's front door. It was facing the street.

Linuxカーネルに新たな脆弱性「NoisyTCP」（CVE-2026-99288）。

TCP通信の処理に欠陥があり、条件が揃うと、外部から認証なしでLinuxサーバーをカーネルごと停止させられる可能性があります。

nginx、Apache、SSHなど、個々のサービスの脆弱性ではなく、Linuxカーネル自体の問題です。

【11月27日現在の修正状況】

・Amazon Linux 2023：修正版公開済み
・Debian 12／13：修正版公開済み
・Ubuntu：16.04から26.10までの標準カーネルが未修正

Ubuntuは現時点で最新の標準カーネルに更新しても、今回の脆弱性は解消されません。

修正版が公開されるまでは、不要なTCPポートの外部公開を停止し、SSHなどの管理用ポートへのアクセスを許可IPに限定してください。

また、10月に公表されたTCPの脆弱性（CVE-2026-98432）とは別の欠陥です。

私が管理しているサーバーも11月上旬にカーネルを更新したばかりですが、Amazon Linux 2023の環境は再度更新します。Ubuntuの環境は修正版の公開待ちです。

まず、現在稼働しているカーネルを確認してください。

uname -r

Docker環境でも、更新が必要なのはコンテナではなくホストOSのカーネルです。更新後は再起動し、修正済みのカーネルが稼働していることを確認してください。

今回の脆弱性による影響はサービス停止（DoS）であり、情報漏洩や任意コード実行ではありません。

Ubuntuの修正版の公開状況は公式サイトで確認できます。

An attacker patched a vulnerability on its own relay server. That is the detail I keep coming back to in GreyNoise's writeup of the Check Point campaign.

GreyNoise tracked an intrusion campaign against Check Point Security Management Servers hitting at least 22 organizations between October 17 and November 2. The actor used a compromised server as an operational relay, staging stolen firewall databases and internal CA files there.

By early November, other threat actors were scanning the relay. The actor ran a check for CVE-2026-98432, a Linux IPv4 use-after-free, then used nftables to drop the packet types that trigger it. Per GreyNoise: 'This allowed the actor to protect their hop from others engaging in future exploitation of the bug.'

Defender takeaway: attacker infrastructure gets patch hygiene too, and that shows up on your side. Unexpected nftables rules on a server nobody should be tuning, or an entry in /etc/ld.so.preload, are worth alerting on. The victims here only got identified because the actor's automation failed and shipped error output back to the hop.

19 years of BitLocker lockout just collapsed to 20 days because of a $1 motherboard flash chip.

Firmware TPMs on modern laptops store failed PIN counts on external SPI flash. TPM 2.0 Dictionary Attack Protection enforces a 32-try limit followed by one guess every 10 minutes, relying on a JEDEC counter called RPMC inside that flash chip to stop state rollbacks.

 At ACM CCS 2026, researchers broke that lock on both sides.
On Winbond RPMC flash (25R and 74M chips), a 1-second voltage glitch leaks the HMAC signing key straight out of the chip. Any laptop using that flash, Intel or AMD, now accepts forged counter values and rolls back its failed-attempt state.

On AMD fTPM (CVE-2026-43613), the firmware skips verifying whether the counter ever incremented. A custom interposer sitting between the CPU and SPI flash blocks counter updates with zero glitching.

 Measured worst-case brute-force results on locked laptops:
  * 4-digit Windows Hello PIN: 69 days down to 40 hours
  * 6-digit BitLocker startup PIN: 19 years down to 20 days

Winbond has no patch timeline because fixing the leak takes new silicon. AMD published AMD-SB-7079 with firmware fixes rolling out from November 2026 through February 2027.

Researchers used a flash-chip interposer to bypass TPM lockout and guess Hello and BitLocker PINs in lab tests; AMD tracks CVE-2026-43613 (CVSS 5.1). Check devices for tampering; lengthen PINs.

Your PC has a mechanism that remembers every incorrect PIN attempt and eventually locks you out

Researchers at TU Berlin found a way to make that mechanism forget

Their attack, called Hello Again, targets the Replay Protected Monotonic Counters (RPMC) used to protect security state stored in motherboard flash memory

The TPM relies on this state to remember failed authentication attempts and prevent brute-force guessing

The researchers found two ways to undermine that protection:

On affected AMD systems, they intercepted communication between the processor and flash chip, suppressing counter updates while making the processor believe they succeeded
On systems using vulnerable Winbond flash chips, voltage glitching exposed a cryptographic key that allowed the researchers to forge counter values

With the lockout state repeatedly reset, they could automate PIN guesses without the normal security delays

Their laboratory demonstrations included:

A four-digit Windows Hello PIN found in 57 minutes, with a worst-case estimated search time of 40 hours instead of 69 days
A six-digit BitLocker startup PIN found in under seven minutes, with a worst-case estimate of 20 days instead of 19 years

The attack required physical access, specialised hardware and vulnerable hardware configurations

It also affects different platforms for different reasons

AMD assigned its firmware issue CVE-2026-43613 and is planning firmware fixes extending into February 2027

Intel says the research did not demonstrate a vulnerability in Intel components; the tested Intel system depended on a flaw in its third-party Winbond flash chip

For now, researchers recommend using longer PINs, adding at least two digits where possible

The deeper security lesson is that a PIN's strength depends not only on how difficult it is to guess, but also on whether the hardware enforcing guess limits can be trusted

The campaign exploited PHP2Shell vulnerabilities CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, with an operator adapting public proofs of concept on the day they appeared. The custom exploit reportedly worked against default PHP/Apache configurations: a multipart POST with more than 1,000 fields and excessive header lines exhausted PHP’s memory limit, while a second request on the same keep-alive connection used residual session state to leak memory and invoke `system`. The exploit supported PHP builds through per-version calibration, but patched releases stopped the chain. The reported fixes are PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12.

The operator fingerprinted PHP/Apache hosts using Shodan, narrowing a pool of 68,198 hosts to a shortlist of about 5,042. The campaign targeted 595 unique IPs across 57 countries; 404 hosts were assessed as compromised, with approximately 290,000 files (9.5 GB) collected. Exploitation and collection were organized through a job-based C2 and an AI-agent system: a custom queue dispatched 39 workers backed by two self-hosted DeepSeek endpoints. The evidence indicates human-directed, AI-assisted operations; complete autonomous execution was not established.

Post-compromise activity included reverse shells, SSH-key installation, periodic beacons, token-protected PHP webshells, cron persistence, and localhost-only Dropbear tunnels. Collection scripts inventoried hosts, searched repositories for secrets, gathered database backups and application data, and harvested cloud credentials, OAuth tokens, session files, and source code. Stolen credentials enabled cloud enumeration and further access attempts. A separate financial-fraud effort reached withdrawal and account-takeover capabilities, but no cryptocurrency theft was confirmed; an unauthenticated Redis instance did yield about 3.3 million user records.

Defenders should investigate suspicious high-volume multipart PHP requests followed by a same-connection request, web-server processes spawning shells or download tools, new SSH keys, unauthorized PHP prepend directives, Dropbear on loopback, and outbound traffic to the reported C2 on port 8088 or reverse-shell ports 41000–49153. Patching alone is insufficient after compromise: affected hosts require investigation or reimaging, and exposed credentials should be rotated. The report does not attribute the activity to a known threat group.

Three exposed directories contained evidence of an active intrusion crew’s operations. A large US hospital system’s material included staff credentials, 8,460 email addresses, an authentication dump, a web-server `phpinfo` capture, and a separately recorded VPN session. The records do not prove a successful domain login, patient-data loss, or continuous VPN access. A US manufacturer’s Azure blob container was enumerated using a live SAS token, yielding 155,568 object names, including QuickBooks files; the files indicate listing, not downloading. The crew also ran the manufacturer’s Windows hashes against a custom wordlist.

The toolkit included FortiGate credential checking and a probe for the FortiOS LDAP empty-password bypass CVE-2026-22153, plus scripts for Exchange MRSProxy pre-auth RCE (CVE-2026-62911), TightVNC (CVE-2024-42049), and an LFI vulnerability (CVE-2026-87902). Other available tools included Impacket, Responder, PetitPotam, krbrelayx, PKINITtools, mitm6, and NetExec. Their presence does not establish successful use against named targets.

A malicious Java JDBC provider, `https://t.co/ls1A1701Aa.sqlserver.jdbc.TlsChannelFix`, runs code when loaded. A separate launcher XOR-decodes a file and starts a 2.1 MB Windows executable with components consistent with an Apollo-derived payload. A 7.7 MB Linux ELF was identified as a Poseidon implant. The crew also used custom Java HTTPS beaconing and clients for Net Monitor for Employees Professional over authenticated SOCKS relays. Reconnaissance output was base64-encoded and exfiltrated in chunks through HTTP GET request paths.

The files also contained 35,601 Kerberos key records across 11,867 principals from a Bangladeshi university and staged domain database and registry hives from a Swiss tax office. Hundreds of US law firms and several federal agencies were enumerated, but these are targets, not confirmed compromises. Credential-stuffing and exploit attempts against one law firm showed failures. Активность выявила GreyNoise, отметившая, что она напоминает операции кибершпионажа, хотя мотивы злоумышленника окончательно установить не удалось.

Исследователи отслеживают активность под номером GT13 и подтвердили, что она продолжалась с 17 октября по 2 ноября, после чего их наблюдение прекратилось.

Однако, учитывая постоянный доступ злоумышленника к устройствам Check Point, они считают, что кампания остается активной.

По данным GreyNoise, 22 организации-жертвы расположены в 17 странах, среди которых госучреждения, поставщики финансовых услуг, а также компании энергетического, транспортного, горнодобывающего и производственного секторов.

Атаки были совершены с 99 IP, которые, судя по всему, принадлежат скомпрометированным устройствам Check Point и выходным узлам ExpressVPN.

Файловый HTTP-сервер Rejetto, скомпрометированный с помощью CVE-2026-61500, использовался в качестве оперативного ретранслятора для управления вторжениями и сбора украденных данных из скомпрометированных сред.

GreyNoise пока не смогла установить, когда и как были взломаны серверы Check Point, но зафиксировала использование CVE-2026-16232 на этапах после взлома.

Уязвимость связана с обходом аутентификации в Check Point SmartConsole, которая позволяет злоумышленникам получить токен для входа в приложение и пройти аутентификацию с правами администратора.

В свою очередь, Check Point предупредила о ней еще в июле, обозначив ее как активно используемую 0-day.

Исследователи также зафиксировали попытки использования CVE-2025-5777 (Citrix NetScaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti), CVE-2026-41089 (Windows NetLogon), CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole) и CVE-2026-98432 (Linux IPv4 UAF).

26 октября злоумышленник провел операцию по массовому управлению сертификатами на всех 24 скомпрометированных серверах Check Point, которая завершилась неудачей, но зато помогла GreyNoise идентифицировать жертв.

Исследователи пришли к выводу, что GT13 использовала инструмент нападения на основе ИИ, основываясь на поведении, наблюдаемой автоматизации и специально разработанных инструментах, однако использование ИИ в этой кампании остается неподтвержденным.

Учитывая, что кампания все еще может быть активной, GreyNoise поделилась IOCs, которые могут помочь выявить дополнительные вторжения или заблокировать будущие попытки.

Представители Check Point заявляют, что им известно о действиях, описанных в отчете GreyNoise.

По их данным, злоумышленники использовали CVE-2026-16232, позволяющую обойти аутентификацию SmartConsole, о которой Check Point публично сообщила в июле 2026 года, отметив, что эксплуатация уже наблюдалась в реальных условиях.

Таким образом, эта уязвимость и доступные средства защиты не являются новыми. Злоумышленники также использовали адаптированный общедоступный модуль Metasploit для CVE-2026-16232, поэтому метод эксплуатации уже был известен ранее.

The report describes misuse of ARTEX, an LLM-powered penetration-testing framework, across several campaigns. Reported activity includes attacks against South Korean financial organizations, Japanese companies, IT and software vendors, and financial-sector targets. The operators remain unknown in the Korean and Japanese cases; the report treats them as separate intrusions and does not infer shared attribution from overlapping infrastructure. Storm-0940 activity involved password spraying and abuse of ConnectWise Cloud Backup-related access. Storm-3358 activity involved financial-sector targeting and infrastructure associated with WISP. Other reported tools include vshell and AdaptixC2.

Common behaviors include rapid reconnaissance of web and API surfaces; enumeration of distinct customer or application records; probing authentication, SSO, OAuth, and application endpoints; and password spraying with rotating user agents. Other patterns include repeated requests with altered headers or tokens, SSRF attempts using redirecting URLs to reach internal or metadata addresses, and downloading exposed configuration or backup files. Cloud activity includes exposed-secret use, service-principal sign-ins, OAuth credential addition, and credential discovery across AWS services. The report also describes upload-then-execute behavior and self-correcting API retries, including retries after HTTP 422 responses.

The detection approach prioritizes behavior over framework-specific strings, which can be changed or generated by the model. Proposed rules correlate sequences such as multiple distinct reconnaissance requests within a short window, high-volume record access, and file uploads followed by execution. ARTEX-specific headers, user agents, webshell keys, response markers, domains, and IP addresses are treated as supporting indicators; shared infrastructure and generic user agents require caution. Threat actors are actively exploiting vulnerabilities in Ivanti Connect Secure and Ivanti Policy Secure gateways, affecting supported 9.x and 22.x versions. CVE-2023-46805 enables authentication bypass, while CVE-2024-21887 allows command injection; chained exploitation can provide unauthenticated remote code execution with elevated privileges. CVE-2024-21893 is a SAML server-side request forgery flaw that can expose restricted resources without authentication. The advisory also identifies CVE-2024-22024, an XML vulnerability in the SAML component, and CVE-2024-21888, a privilege-escalation flaw.

After gaining access, attackers have deployed web shells including GLASSTOKEN, GIFTEDVISITOR, BUSHWALK, LIGHTWIRE, and CHAINLINE to execute commands on compromised appliances. Investigations found attackers harvesting credentials stored on the gateways, including cached Active Directory administrator credentials, cleartext passwords and NTLM hashes associated with active sessions, and credentials recovered from database backups. They have used appliance-native tools and libraries, including FreeRDP, SSH, Telnet, and Nmap, for internal reconnaissance and lateral movement; some incidents resulted in domain compromise. Observed post-exploitation activity also included deploying a Sliver implant.

CISA research demonstrated that root-level access could be used to establish persistence that survives factory resets and upgrades. Persistence stored on an encrypted drive partition may evade integrity checks. CISA investigations found web shells on devices that the Ivanti Integrity Checker Tool (ICT) reported as having no file mismatches. Attackers were also observed overwriting and time-stomping files and remounting the runtime partition, further obscuring evidence of compromise. Therefore, a clean ICT result or device reset does not reliably establish that an appliance is uncompromised.

Defenders should treat credentials stored on affected appliances as potentially exposed, hunt for malicious activity, apply available Ivanti updates, and assess the risk of continued appliance use. Recommended exposure-reduction measures include restricting appliance outbound connections to required services and limiting VPN access to unprivileged accounts.

🚨 MITRE Technique Spotlight: T1190 — Exploit Public-Facing Application

Initial access doesn't always require phishing. Adversaries increasingly target internet-facing infrastructure—web apps, VPNs, firewalls, and email gateways—to gain their first foothold.

Recent campaigns show this trend clearly: MOVEit Transfer exploitation (CVE-2023-34362) by Cl0p ransomware gang, Citrix Bleed (CVE-2023-4966) enabling session hijacking, and Ivanti Connect Secure vulnerabilities (CVE-2024-21887) chained for pre-auth RCE. These aren't theoretical—they're active, widespread, and devastating.

Detection requires layered visibility:
• WAF logs showing SQL injection, path traversal, or deserialization attempts
• IDS/IPS signatures firing on exploit payloads
• Web server access logs with anomalous POST requests, unusual user-agents, or 200 responses to non-existent paths
• EDR alerts on unexpected child processes from w3wp.exe, httpd, tomcat, or java.exe
• Webshell indicators: aspx/jsp/php files in web directories with eval(), base64_decode(), or cmd.exe execution

Log sources: IIS logs (W3C format), Apache access/error logs, Sysmon Event ID 1 (process creation) from web server hosts, firewall connection logs, and application-specific logs (e.g., Tomcat catalina[.]out).

Patch management isn't sexy, but it's your first line of defense. Vulnerability scanning must cover external attack surface continuously—not quarterly.

The evidence base distinguishes three tiers of AI-discovered vulnerability claims, and they carry different confidence levels.

The first tier — software and library vulnerabilities — is well-documented. Google GTIG tracked 2,076 AI-related CVEs between January 2025 and August 2026, with more than 1,500 in 2026 alone, roughly half affecting AI orchestration frameworks [Source: SecurityWeek / Google GTIG, Sep 30, 2026]. One named example, CVE-2026-1731, was an unauthenticated OS command injection flaw in BeyondTrust Privileged Remote Access discovered autonomously by the Hacktron AI research agent; one threat cluster exploited it within four days of public disclosure, and five more followed within seven days [Source: SecurityWeek / Google GTIG, Sep 30, 2026]. The Axios reporting on early testing of new frontier models describes Cisco and Zscaler using them internally to "chain together vulnerabilities to build an exploit chain" — the shift from single-bug discovery to multi-step attack path construction [Source: Axios, Apr 21, 2026].

The second tier — kernel and root-access flaws — is documented at one confirmed instance. Between April 29 and May 13, 2026, three publicly disclosed flaws gave local users a path to root access across major Linux distributions. Microsoft confirmed that AI found the "Copy Fail" vulnerability among them, and assessed that "the other two fit the same broader pattern, suggesting that AI will increase the pace at which serious vulnerability classes are discovered" [Source: Microsoft MDDR, Oct 9, 2026]. Kernel-level access is the layer immediately above hardware — it controls hardware, memory, and system processes. An attacker who compromises the kernel gains, in Microsoft's words, "total dominion over the system." This is the closest documented open-source analogue to what Altman describes as "hardware-level, insane stuff."

The third tier — structurally unpatchable hardware vulnerabilities, Altman's specific claim — is where open-source evidence runs thin. The Mother Jones piece notes that a PHP vulnerability type had been "noted decades ago, but the flaw had been considered too difficult to exploit and was largely forgotten until August [2026], when researchers using new models found a way to exploit it" [Source: Mother Jones, Oct 21, 2026]. This describes a class of vulnerability where the flaw was known but assumed to be beyond exploitation — AI changed the feasibility calculation, not the patching requirement. That is distinct from hardware bugs that physically cannot be patched. Altman's statement remains the primary public evidence for the hardware-unpatchable category; no independent technical source corroborates it with specifics in the collected evidence. 1/6

vulnerabilities.description: A flaw was found in pam. When built with libeconf and an unconfigured vendor directory, the pam econf configuration handler misinterprets the search path, causing it to look for configuration files in a relative directory within the current working directory. A local attacker can exploit this by placing crafted environment configuration files in a world-writable location. If an administrator executes a privileged command from that directory, the malicious variables are loaded into the privileged process, resulting in local privilege escalation.

ntfy before v2.38.3 contains a server-side request forgery vulnerability that allows remote attackers to bypass the web push endpoint allow-list by crafting a URL containing '#' or '?' characters that satisfy the [^/]+ regex pattern used to validate mozaws.net and notify.windows.com hosts. Attackers can submit an endpoint .example#.mozaws.net/push, which passes validation while Go parses the actual host as attacker.example, causing the server to send subsequent web push POST requests to an attacker-controlled or internal host.

Allocation of resources without limits or throttling vulnerability in Apache Tomcat during HTTP upgrade in some circumstances lead to possible DoS.



This issue affects Apache Tomcat: from 11.0.0 through 11.0.27, from 10.1.0 through 10.1.61, from 9.0.41 through 9.0.123.



The following versions were EOL at the time the CVE was created but are known to be affected: from 8.5.61 through 8.5.100. Other unsupported versions may also be affected.



Users are recommended to upgrade to version 11.0.29, 10.1.62 or 9.0.124, which fix the issue.
Note: Tomcat 11.0.28 was not released

An issue was discovered in HAProxy 3.3.0 through 3.4.4 and in 3.5-dev1 through 3.5-dev5. Exploitation requires an HTTP/3 frontend: HAProxy must be built with QUIC support and configured with a QUIC bind listener, and the affected traffic must reach a backend over HTTP/1.1 using chunked transfer coding on a reused connection. Under those conditions, when an HTTP/3 request carries no Content-Length header, the HTTP/3 multiplexer credits the length declared in a DATA frame header to the stream endpoint's known-input-payload estimate at the moment the frame header is decoded, before the payload has been received, and that declared length is emitted verbatim as the HTTP/1.1 chunk size. A remote unauthenticated client that declares more payload than it delivers and then ends the stream causes HAProxy to announce a chunk larger than the bytes it writes and to return the connection to the idle pool in a desynchronized state. The result is potential HTTP request smuggling on reused backend connections: an attacker can place a request past a frontend rule such as a path-based http-request deny, so that the smuggled request is never seen by HAProxy's HTTP analysis, and can cause concurrent clients' requests, including their request lines and Authorization headers, to be consumed as the attacker's request body and lost. Exploitation is not deterministic; it depends on a race with backend connection pooling, succeeding in a majority of but not all trials during testing, and can be retried freely. The mechanism was introduced in 3.3-dev10; releases 3.2.x and earlier are unaffected.

bigcommerce-api-mcp before 1.0.1 contains a missing authentication vulnerability that allows remote unauthenticated attackers to invoke MCP tools because the /sse and /messages routes skip the authenticateRequest middleware. Attackers can open /sse to obtain a session id and POST JSON-RPC tool calls to /messages to retrieve store product, order and customer records using the operator's BigCommerce API key.

A security flaw has been discovered in eosphoros-ai DB-GPT up to 0.8.3. This affects the function editor sql run of the file packages/dbgpt-app/src/dbgpt app/openapi/api v1/editor/api editor v1.py of the component Editor SQL Run API. Performing a manipulation of the argument db name results in authorization bypass. It is possible to initiate the attack remotely. The exploit has been released to the public and may be used for attacks. The pull request to fix this issue awaits acceptance.

Bagel (bagel-mcp) before 2.5.5 contains an argument injection vulnerability in RsyncFilesToLocalDirectory that allows attackers to inject rsync options because only --quiet and --log-format values are rejected. Attackers who influence the LLM through prompt-injected content can trigger run pipeline with -e/--rsh or --rsync-path options to execute commands as the Bagel server process.

WhoDB from 0.88.0 before 0.132.0 contains an access control bypass in the MCP whodb query tool, letting callers run file-writing statements without approval because the sqlguard keyword classifier omits INTO, OUTFILE and DUMPFILE. MCP clients or prompt-injected models can execute PostgreSQL lo export or MySQL SELECT INTO OUTFILE to create files on the database host and create tables, bypassing confirmation and read-only modes.

mcp-video-analyzer 0.2.0 before 0.10.1 contains a server-side request forgery vulnerability that allows attackers to reach internal addresses by supplying any http(s) URL ending in a video extension. Attackers can use prompt injection to make tools like get frames fetch loopback, private, or cloud metadata addresses directly or via redirects, writing responses to disk or returning rendered screenshots.

Wazuh-MCP-Server before commit 2bbfe12 contains a server-side request forgery vulnerability in the blueteam check webshell tool because WebshellCheckInput.validate url accepts DNS hostnames without resolving them. Attackers can supply URLs whose hostnames resolve or redirect to loopback, private, or link-local addresses, making curl reach internal services and cloud metadata endpoints and leak response details.

A vulnerability has been identified in Mendix OIDC Provider (Mendix 10 compatible) (All versions < V6.0.0), Mendix OIDC Provider (Mendix 11 compatible) (All versions < V6.0.0), Mendix OIDC Provider (Mendix 9 compatible) (All versions < V4.3.0). Affected versions of the module do not properly validate the integrity of JWTs submitted to the OIDC Provider Token Introspection endpoint, allowing tokens to be associated with legitimate token records based solely on their jti value.

This could allow unauthenticated remote attackers to hijack an account (session) when gaining access to an jti of an active token.

The Upsell Funnel Builder for WooCommerce – Create Upsells, Cross-Sells, Order Bumps, Frequently Bought, and Popups. plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'form data' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 3.1.7 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. The nonce gating the vulnerable AJAX endpoint is publicly emitted to any visitor loading a cart, checkout, or shortcode page, making the endpoint fully exploitable by unauthenticated attackers without any prior account or login.

Typebot from 2.14.0 before 3.19.0 contains an authorization flaw that allows authenticated bot authors to reference another workspace's legacy webhook by saving a foreign webhookId in an HTTP request block. Attackers can have executeHttpRequestBlock return the victim's URL, headers and body client-side, or use handleSubscribeHttpRequest to overwrite the victim's webhook URL and redirect its data.

The Database for Contact Form 7, WPforms, Elementor forms plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Arbitrary File Upload in all versions up to, and including, 1.5.5 via the copy files function. This is due to missing file extension validation in the copy files function, which accepts attacker-controlled stream wrapper URIs as the file source and derives the destination filename without restricting executable extensions. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to upload files that may be executable, which makes remote code execution possible. The plugin places an .htaccess file in its uploads directory to block PHP execution, but this mitigation is ineffective on Nginx, LiteSpeed in certain configurations, and Apache servers with AllowOverride None, and the file is not restored if deleted.

The Sneeit Framework plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Remote Code Execution in versions up to, and including, 8.7 via the 'callback' parameter of the sneeit compact menu mega content AJAX action. The handler sneeit compact menu mega content callback() is registered on the wp ajax nopriv hook and passes the attacker-supplied 'callback' value directly into call user func() after only a function exists() check, with the single argument also attacker-controlled via a JSON-decoded 'args' parameter. There is no authentication, no capability check, no nonce, and no allow-list of callable functions. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary existing PHP/WordPress functions with controlled arguments.

Dreamweaver Desktop is affected by a Dependency on Vulnerable Third-Party Component vulnerability that could result in arbitrary code execution in the context of the current user. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability to execute arbitrary code. Exploitation depends on conditions beyond the attacker's control and requires user interaction in that a victim must open a malicious file. Scope is changed.

The system call verifier z vrfy k thread stack space get() in kernel/thread.c checked the result of K SYSCALL OBJ(thread, K OBJ THREAD) with the CHECKIF() macro instead of K OOPS(). CHECKIF() compiles to if (0) when CONFIG NO RUNTIME CHECKS is selected, and becomes an assertion when CONFIG ASSERT ON ERRORS is selected. In both cases, the kernel-object validation result for the user-supplied thread pointer is ignored, or is a no-op when assertions are disabled.

On builds with CONFIG USERSPACE, CONFIG INIT STACKS and CONFIG THREAD STACK INFO plus one of those check modes, a user-mode thread can call k thread stack space get() with an arbitrary pointer. That pointer can be a fake struct k thread in its own memory, or a thread object it has no permission on. z impl k thread stack space get() then dereferences thread->stack info in supervisor mode and scans memory starting at the attacker-chosen stack info.start.

The syscall returns the number of leading 0xAA bytes at that address. This gives an unprivileged thread a limited oracle on arbitrary kernel or peripheral memory, and allows privileged reads of attacker-selected addresses, including MMIO. No write primitive results. The default CONFIG RUNTIME ERROR CHECKS configuration is not affected. The fix replaces the CHECKIF() with K OOPS() so the object check is always enforced.

Zettlr before 4.11.0 fails to validate URI schemes in Markdown link targets, allowing attackers to launch arbitrary registered protocol handlers via Electron shell.openExternal without confirmation. Attackers can craft documents whose Ctrl/Cmd-clicked links use smb:// to leak NTLM credential hashes on Windows or invoke custom protocol handlers with attacker-controlled parameters.
